column4: Building on our study of Jesus as the Messiah, in this chapter we continue in looking at the life, person, and work of Jesus. We’ll see that Jesus is the Mediator of a new and better covenant-and that He perfectly fills the roles of Prophet, Priest, and King. It is in this New Covenant that we as believers have good standing with God and transition from a works-based covenant to a trust-based (faith-based) covenant. Finally, we will read and study the *Apostles Creed* as a way to round-out our study on Jesus.
column5: Continuing our study of Jesus as the Christ, in this chapter we continue to look at Jesus’s life, character, and work. We will see that Jesus is the mediator of a new and better covenant-and that he perfectly fulfills the roles of prophet, priest, and king. In this new covenant we, as believers, are in good standing with God and move from a works-based covenant to a trust-based (faith-based) covenant. Finally, as a way to wrap up our study on Jesus, we will read and study the Apostles’ Creed.

column4: ## Mediator of the New Covenant
column5: ## Mediator of the New Covenant

column4: The concept of a mediator involves a go-between who bridges the gap between two parties, facilitating a relationship or agreement. In the Exodus story, Moses is the initial mediator of the covenant God established with His people. Moses received the law, offered the sacrifice (priest), called God’s people to obedience (prophet), and judged them (judge / king). In the remainder of the Old Testament after Moses, the mediating role was fulfilled through the role of the Prophet, the Levitical Priesthood, and the Judges and later Kings of the nation.
column5: The concept of a mediator involves the role of a go-between who bridges the gap between two parties and makes a relationship or agreement possible. In the story of Exodus, Moses is the initial mediator who represented the covenant God made with his people. Moses received the Law, offered sacrifices (priest), called God’s people to obedience (prophet), and judged them (judge / king). After Moses, the rest of the Old Testament sees the role of mediator carried out by the prophets, the Levitical priesthood, and by the judges and later the nation’s kings.

column4: Old Testament Roles of Mediators:
column5: Roles of mediators in the Old Testament:

column4: 1.  **Prophet:** Prophets were God’s messengers, sent to speak His heart to the people and call them back when they wandered. Moses, for example, served as a prophet who mediated the Old Covenant by receiving the Law from God and teaching it to Israel. Prophets also foretold the coming of the Messiah and the ultimate redemption of humanity. Other prominent examples of prophet include: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Elijah, Elisha, Samuel.
column5: 1.  **Prophet:** Prophets were God’s messengers, sent to convey his will to the people and to call them back when they strayed. For example, Moses functioned as a prophet who, having received the Law from God and taught Israel, mediated the old covenant. The prophets also foretold the coming of the Messiah and the final redemption of humanity. Other prominent examples of prophets are: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Elijah, Elisha, Samuel.

column4: 2.  **Levitical Priesthood:** Priests acted as mediators by offering sacrifices for the atonement of sins and interceding for the people before God. The High Priest, especially, played a vital role on the Day of Atonement, entering the Holy of Holies to sprinkle blood on the mercy seat, symbolizing reconciliation with God. The priest's ministry is to intercede for the people.
column5: 2.  **Levitical priesthood:** The priests acted as mediators by offering sacrifices for the atonement of sins and by interceding before God on behalf of the people. In particular, the high priest played an important role on the Day of Atonement, entering the Holy of Holies and sprinkling blood on the mercy seat, which symbolized reconciliation with God. The ministry of the priest is to intercede for the people.

column4: 3.  **Judge/King:** Judges, and later Kings, were charged with ruling over God’s people, enforcing His laws, judging between the people, delivering them from their enemies, and leading them in righteousness. The book of Judges tells the stories of these leaders-people like Deborah, Samson, and Gideon-whom God raised up to rescue and guide Israel. Israel later had a line of kings, many wicked, some good (see 1st and 2nd Kings, 1st and 2nd Samuel, and 1<sup>st</sup> and 2<sup>nd</sup> Chronicles). Some prominent examples are Saul, David, and Solomon.
column5: 3.  **Judge/king:** The judges and later the kings were charged with ruling over God’s people, enforcing his statutes, judging among the people, delivering them from their enemies, and leading them in righteousness. The book of Judges tells the stories of these leaders—people like Deborah, Samson, and Gideon—whom God raised up to save and guide Israel. Later there was a series of kings in Israel—many evil, some good (see 1st and 2nd Kings, 1st and 2nd Samuel, and 1<sup>st</sup> and 2<sup>nd</sup> Chronicles). Some key examples are Saul, David, and Solomon.

column4: Worth noting is that all the Old Covenant mediators were fully man and not divine. As men they were able to sin, and many times were given to sin. Some of the mediators were sinful and drove people away from God and towards profane worship: false prophets, lying and corrupt priests, and wicked kings.
column5: Notably, all the mediators of the old covenant were entirely human, not divine. Being human, they could sin, and many times they did fall into sin. Some mediators were sinful and led the people away from God into profane worship: false prophets, false and corrupt priests, and wicked kings.

column4: ### Christ as the Mediator of the New Covenant
column5: ### Christ as the mediator of the New Covenant

column4: Jesus’ death, resurrection and ascension fulfil the Old Covenant, and establish the New Covenant.
column5: Jesus’s death, resurrection, and ascension fulfill the old covenant and establish the new covenant.

column4: The New Covenant is a transformative relationship between God and His people, established through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Unlike the Old Covenant, which was focused on external laws, the New Covenant emphasizes internal transformation and grace. It was inaugurated by Jesus at the Last Supper, where He declared that His blood would establish this covenant, replacing the repeated animal sacrifices of the Old Covenant with His once-for-all atonement (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 9:12; Hebrews 10:10). Through this sacrifice, the New Covenant provides complete forgiveness and cleansing from sin, fulfilling the requirement for a perfect and permanent reconciliation with God (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:12; Hebrews 10:12-18).
column5: The new covenant is a transformative relationship between God and his people, established through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. In contrast to the old covenant, which focused on external regulations, the new covenant emphasizes inner transformation and grace. Jesus inaugurated this covenant at the Last Supper, where he declared that his blood would establish it, replacing the repeated animal sacrifices of the old covenant with his once-for-all atonement (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 9:12; Hebrews 10:10). Through this sacrifice, the new covenant provides full forgiveness and cleansing from sin, meeting the need for perfect and lasting reconciliation with God (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:12; Hebrews 10:12-18).

column4: One of the central features of the New Covenant is its internal nature, as God writes His law on the hearts of His people, fostering a heart-level relationship with Him through the Holy Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10; 2 Corinthians 3:3). This shift enables believers to live out God’s will not by mere adherence to external commands but through empowerment by the Spirit (Romans 8:1-4). The New Covenant also grants direct access to God, eliminating the need for an earthly priesthood. Jesus serves as the eternal High Priest, and believers are called a royal priesthood, able to confidently approach God through Christ’s sacrifice (Hebrews 7:24-25; Hebrews 10:19-20; 1 Peter 2:9).
column5: One of the chief features of the new covenant is its internal nature, as God writes his law on the hearts of his people, establishing a heart-level relationship with them through the Holy Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10; 2 Corinthians 3:3). This transformation moves believers beyond merely keeping external commandments and enables them, by the power of the Spirit, to live out God’s will (Romans 8:1-4). The new covenant also grants direct access to God, ending the need for an earthly priesthood. Jesus is the eternal High Priest, and believers are called a royal priesthood, who can approach God with boldness through Christ’s sacrifice (Hebrews 7:24-25; Hebrews 10:19-20; 1 Peter 2:9).

column4: Unlike the Old Covenant, which was exclusive to Israel, the New Covenant is universal, extending to all who believe in Christ, regardless of ethnicity or background (John 3:16; Galatians 3:28). This covenant is based entirely on grace, offering salvation and forgiveness freely through faith in Jesus (Ephesians 2:8-9). It is not sustained by human effort but by the enabling power of the Holy Spirit, who transforms and empowers believers to live in obedience and reflect God’s character (Ezekiel 36:26-27; Romans 8:9-16; Galatians 5:22-23). Furthermore, the New Covenant is everlasting, surpassing the temporary and conditional nature of the Old Covenant (Jeremiah 32:40; Hebrews 8:13). It represents the ultimate fulfillment of God’s redemptive plan, reconciling humanity to Himself and enabling believers to live as His people under His rule for eternity.
column5: In contrast to the old covenant, which was limited to Israel, the new covenant is universal—it extends to everyone who believes in Christ, regardless of ethnicity or background (John 3:16; Galatians 3:28). This covenant is entirely based on grace, freely granting salvation and forgiveness through faith in Jesus (Ephesians 2:8-9). It is not sustained by human effort, but by the empowering work of the Holy Spirit—who transforms believers and enables them to live in obedience and reflect God’s character (Ezekiel 36:26-27; Romans 8:9-16; Galatians 5:22-23). At the same time, the new covenant is eternal, surpassing the temporary and conditional nature of the old covenant (Jeremiah 32:40; Hebrews 8:13). It represents the ultimate fulfillment of God’s plan of salvation—reconciling humanity to himself and enabling believers to live forever under his rule as his people.

column4: Through His atoning death and resurrection, Christ inaugurates this new covenant, replacing the old system of sacrifices and external laws with a covenant written on the hearts of believers (Jeremiah 31:31-34). He stands between God and humanity, not only interceding on behalf of His people but also providing the means of reconciliation through His own blood (Hebrews 9:12). Unlike the mediators of the Old Covenant, Jesus is sinless, eternal, and fully capable of fulfilling the divine requirements for justice and mercy, ensuring a lasting relationship between God and believers.
column5: By his atoning death and resurrection, Christ inaugurates this new covenant, which replaces the old system of sacrifices and external regulations with a covenant written on the hearts of believers (Jeremiah 31:31-34). He stands between God and humanity—not only interceding on behalf of his people, but also providing, by his own blood, the means of reconciliation (Hebrews 9:12). Unlike the mediators of the old covenant, Jesus is sinless and eternal, fully able to meet the divine requirements of justice and mercy, thus securing a lasting relationship between God and believers.

column4: Jesus Fulfills and Perfects These Roles
column5: Jesus fulfills and perfects these roles

column4: 1. **Prophet:** Jesus is the ultimate Prophet, not merely a messenger of God’s word but the Word made flesh (John 1:14). He reveals God’s character, will, and plan for salvation fully and perfectly (Hebrews 1:1-2). His teachings, miracles, and prophetic declarations fulfill the Old Testament prophecies and provide the foundation for the New Covenant.
column5: 1. **Prophet:** Jesus is the supreme Prophet; he is not only the messenger of the word of God, but the Word made flesh (John 1:14). He reveals God’s nature, will, and plan of salvation fully and perfectly (Hebrews 1:1-2). His teachings, miracles, and prophetic declarations fulfill the prophecies of the Old Testament and lay the foundation of the New Covenant.

column4: 2. **Priest:** Jesus is the perfect High Priest, offering Himself as the once-for-all sacrifice for sin (Hebrews 7:27). Unlike the priests of the Old Covenant who had to repeatedly offer sacrifices for their own sins and those of the people, Jesus, being sinless, offered His own blood to secure eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:14).
column5: 2. **Priest:** Jesus is the perfect High Priest, who offered himself once for all as a sacrifice for sin (Hebrews 7:27). Unlike the priests of the Old Covenant, who had to offer sacrifices repeatedly for their own sins and for the people’s, Jesus, who is sinless, offered his own blood to secure eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:14).

column4: 3. **King & Judge:** Jesus is the eternal King, reigning in righteousness and justice. As the Son of David, He fulfills the promise of an everlasting kingdom (2 Samuel 7:16). His kingship is not merely earthly but cosmic, ruling over all creation and establishing peace through His victory over sin and death (Philippians 2:9-11). Jesus will return as king and judge, and judge ‘both the living and the dead’ (Acts 10:42).
column5: 3. **King & Judge:** Jesus is the eternal King, who reigns in righteousness and justice. As the Son of David, he fulfills the promise of an everlasting kingdom (2 Samuel 7:16). His kingdom is not limited to the earth alone, but is cosmic—he reigns over all creation and establishes peace through his victory over sin and death (Philippians 2:9-11). Jesus will return as King and Judge, and will judge ‘both the living and the dead’ (Acts 10:42).

column4: In Christ, the roles of Prophet, Priest, and King converge and are fulfilled perfectly. As the Mediator of the New Covenant, He bridges the gap between a holy God and sinful humanity, enabling believers to approach God with confidence (Hebrews 4:16) and ensuring the eternal inheritance promised in Him.
column5: In Christ, the roles of Prophet, Priest, and King come together and are perfectly fulfilled. As the Mediator of the New Covenant, he bridges the gap between the holy God and sinful humanity, enabling believers to draw near to God with boldness (Hebrews 4:16) and securing in him the promised eternal inheritance.

column4: ## The Apostles Creed
column5: ## The Apostles' Creed

column4: The *Apostles Creed* is not found in scripture, it was created and modified based on the earliest teachings of the church. A creed is a formal confession of beliefs, think of it like a pledge or oath combined with a statement of belief. Creeds are important because they are used to unify and separate those who believe in a particular way from those who do not. In the United States it is common at civil functions like city council meetings or legislative gatherings for the attendees to recite the Pledge of Allegiance. The pledge is used widely in the United States, but isn’t used in other countries, because the citizens of those countries do not owe allegiance to the United States. The pledge is not what makes a person ‘American’, but it does represent a significant essential belief for those who are citizens.
column5: *The Apostles' Creed* is not found in Scripture; it was composed and revised from time to time on the basis of the early teachings of the church. A “creed” (statement of faith) is a formal affirmation of beliefs—think of it as a declaration of faith with a pledge or oath. Creeds are important because they both unite those who believe in a particular way and distinguish them from those who do not. In public events such as city council meetings or legislative assemblies in the United States, those present often recite the Pledge of Allegiance. This pledge is widely used in the United States, but not in other countries, because the citizens of those countries do not owe allegiance to the United States. This pledge does not make a person ‘American,’ but for those who are citizens it represents an important foundational belief.

column4: The first recognizable versions of the creed were written in the fourth century A.D. The creed has changed slightly over the centuries, and has slight variations based on the denomination. Not every Christian denomination uses the creed, but in large part it is widely accepted in some form across the whole of Christianity.
column5: The first identifiable versions of this creed were written in the fourth century A.D. Over the centuries the creed has undergone minor changes, and some variations are found depending on denomination. Not every Christian denomination uses this creed, yet in some form it has been widely accepted throughout the Christian world.

column4: The Apostles Creed has been used as a teaching and catechism tool for centuries and communicates the most fundamental truths of the Christian faith, the base beliefs that must be acknowledged and held to be a Christian. Some denominations have a formal catechism process which is how a new believer joins that specific denomination and becomes indoctrinated into their beliefs.
column5: The Apostles’ Creed has been used for centuries as a tool for teaching and catechesis and communicates the most fundamental truths of the Christian faith—the basic beliefs that must be confessed and held in order to be Christian. Some denominations have a formal process of catechesis by which a new believer is incorporated into that particular denomination and instructed in its teachings.

column4: A person does not need to fully understand these beliefs to come to God and receive salvation, salvation is by faith, not by a doctrinal test! However, in continuing in that faith we all should come to understand these fundamental truths.

column4: ## Brief Explanation of the Apostles Creed
column5: ## A brief overview of the Apostles' Creed

column4: The fundamental truths in the Apostles Creed are numerous and quite deep, a full explanation would certainly take many whole volumes to explain. While this chapter is about Jesus, many of the topics cross over into the other members of the Godhead. This will be an abbreviated explanation of the creed, focusing only on the most central themes. Several of these topics are studied in greater depth across the chapters of this book.
column5: The fundamental truths contained in the Apostles’ Creed are many and exceedingly deep; it would indeed take many volumes to give their full description. Although this chapter is about Jesus, many of these topics also relate to the other persons of the Godhead. This is a brief exposition of the creed, focusing only on the most central themes. Many of these topics are explored in greater depth in other chapters of this book.

column4: #### *I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.*
column5: #### *I believe in God, the Father Almighty, Creator of heaven and earth.*

column4: This affirms belief in God as the all-powerful, sovereign Creator and Father. The title "Father" emphasizes God’s loving relationship with His creation, particularly His children through faith (John 1:12). As the Creator, He spoke the universe into existence, bringing order out of chaos (Genesis 1:1-3). His almighty power is displayed in the vastness of creation, while His fatherly care is seen in His ongoing sustenance and providence. This foundational statement establishes God as the origin and ruler of all life, deserving worship and trust.
column5: This affirms belief in God as the Almighty, sovereign Creator and Father. The title “Father” underscores God’s loving relationship with his creation, especially with those who become his children through faith (John 1:12). As Creator, he called the universe into existence by his word, bringing order out of chaos (Genesis 1:1-3). His almighty power is revealed in the vastness of creation, while his fatherly care is seen in its continual preservation and governance. This foundational statement declares God to be the source and ruler of all life, worthy of worship and trust.

column4: #### *I believe in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord.*
column5: #### *I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.*

column4: Jesus Christ is the unique Son of God, eternally begotten, not created, and sharing in the divine nature (John 1:1-2, 14). Jesus is the ‘Word’ since the beginning, and He became flesh and lived with us. As "Christ," He is the anointed Messiah, fulfilling the Old Testament promises of a Savior. The title "Lord" acknowledges His authority over all creation and His rightful position as ruler and King (Philippians 2:10-11). He is not only Lord, but the Lord who saves (Acts 16:31).
column5: Jesus Christ is the unique Son of God—begotten from eternity, not made—and shares in the divine nature (John 1:1-2, 14). Jesus is the Word from the beginning, and he became flesh and dwelt among us. As the “Christ” he is the anointed Messiah who fulfills the Old Testament promises regarding the Savior. The title “Lord” acknowledges his authority over all creation and his rightful place as King and Ruler (Philippians 2:10-11). He is not only Lord, but the Lord who saves (Acts 16:31).

column4: Jesus is not **just** sent from God; He **is** part of God. Jesus abides in the Father and the Father abides in Jesus. The Gospel of John repeatedly establishes that Jesus and the Father are one (John 10:30), that Jesus did not act on His own accord (John 5:19; John 12:49-50), and that everything He did was to glorify His Father (John 17:4; John 14:13), and was done by the authority and power of His Father (John 14:10; John 8:28-29).
column5: Jesus was not **only** sent by God; he **is** a part of him. Jesus abides in the Father and the Father abides in Jesus. The Gospel of John repeatedly proves that Jesus and the Father are one (John 10:30), that Jesus did nothing of himself (John 5:19; John 12:49-50), that whatever he did he did for his Father’s glory (John 17:4; John 14:13), and that all of it was done by his Father’s authority and power (John 14:10; John 8:28-29).

column4: #### *He was conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary.*
column5: #### *He was conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary.*

column4: This affirms the miraculous conception of Jesus through the Holy Spirit, underscoring His divine origin. Born of the Virgin Mary, Jesus fulfills the prophecy of Isaiah 7:14, which foretold the virgin birth of the Messiah. This event marks the incarnation, where the eternal Word of God took on human flesh (John 1:14). By being both fully God and fully human, Jesus bridges the gap between God and humanity, enabling Him to be the perfect mediator and Savior.
column5: This affirms the miraculous conception of Jesus by the Holy Spirit, which underscores his divine origin. By being born of the Virgin Mary, Jesus fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah 7:14, which foretold the virgin birth of the Messiah. This event is the sign of the Incarnation, where the eternal Word of God took on human flesh (John 1:14). Being fully God and fully man, Jesus bridges the gap between God and humanity, making him the perfect Mediator and Savior.

column4: Jesus was conceived by the seed of the Holy Spirit, and did not inherit a sinful nature that we, born of the seed of men, have. Jesus was in every way tempted and tested, but He was perfect and without sin. Hebrews 4:15, 2 Corinthians 5:21, 1 Peter 2:22.
column5: Jesus was conceived by the seed of the Holy Spirit, and he did not inherit the sinful nature that we, who are born of the seed of man, possess. Jesus was tempted and tested in every way, yet he remained perfect and sinless. Hebrews 4:15, 2 Corinthians 5:21, 1 Peter 2:22.

column4: #### *He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.*
column5: #### *He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.*

column4: Jesus’ suffering and death were real, historical events that occurred under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, grounding the Christian faith in verifiable history. His crucifixion was a fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies, such as Isaiah 53:5, which speaks of the Suffering Servant who would bear the sins of many. Jesus’ death was sacrificial, taking the penalty for sin on behalf of humanity (1 Peter 2:24). His burial confirms the reality of His death and prepares for the significance of the resurrection.
column5: Jesus’ suffering and death were real, historical events that occurred under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, grounding the Christian faith in verifiable history. His crucifixion was the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies, such as Isaiah 53:5, which speaks of the suffering servant who would bear the sins of many. Jesus’ death was sacrificial; He took upon Himself the penalty of sin on behalf of humanity (1 Peter 2:24). His burial confirms the reality of His death and sets the stage for the significance of the resurrection.

column4: #### *He descended to the dead.*
column5: #### *He descended to the dead.*

column4: After His death, Jesus descended to the realm of the dead, often referred to as *Hades* or *Sheol* in Scripture. This act demonstrates His full identification with humanity, even in death, and signifies His victory over sin, death, and the devil (1 Peter 3:18-20). By descending, He proclaimed His triumph and the completion of His redemptive work.
column5: After His death, Jesus descended to the realm of the dead, often called Hades or Sheol in Scripture. This act, even in death, demonstrates His complete solidarity with humanity and signals His victory over sin, death, and Satan (1 Peter 3:18-20). By descending He proclaimed His triumph and the completion of His redemptive work.

column4: #### *On the third day He rose again.*
column5: #### *On the third day He rose again.*

column4: The resurrection of Jesus is the cornerstone of our Christian faith, confirming His divinity and the truth of His teachings. By rising from the dead, He defeated sin and death, providing the assurance of eternal life for believers (1 Corinthians 15:17-22). The resurrection also fulfills Scripture, including Jesus’ own predictions (Matthew 16:21). This miraculous event transformed the despair of the disciples into bold faith, forming the foundation of the early Church's witness.
column5: The resurrection of Jesus is the cornerstone of our Christian faith; it confirms His divinity and the truth of His teachings. Rising from the dead, He conquered sin and death and gave believers the assurance of eternal life (1 Corinthians 15:17-22). The resurrection fulfilled both Scripture and Jesus’ own predictions (Matthew 16:21). This miraculous event turned the disciples’ despair into bold faith and laid the foundation for the testimony of the early Church.

column4: #### *He ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of the Father.*
column5: #### *He ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of the Father.*

column4: Jesus’ ascension marks His return to the Father’s presence in glory. Seated at the father’s right hand (Ephesians 1:20), He assumes the role of our eternal High Priest, interceding for believers (Hebrews 7:25). His position of authority also signifies His exaltation as King, reigning over all creation and directing the Church’s mission (Ephesians 1:22) to do greater works (John 14:12) and fulfilling the great commission He gave to us (Matthew 28:18-20, Mark 16:15-18). The ascension assures believers of His ongoing presence and power through the Holy Spirit.
column5: The ascension of Jesus is the sign of His return, in glory, to the Father’s presence. Seated at the Father’s right hand (Ephesians 1:20), He fulfills the role of our eternal High Priest, interceding for believers (Hebrews 7:25). His exalted position also displays His glorification as King—He reigns over all creation and directs the Church’s mission (Ephesians 1:22) so that it may do greater works (John 14:12) and fulfill the Great Commission He gave us (Matthew 28:18-20, Mark 16:15-18). His ascension assures believers of His continuing presence and power through the Holy Spirit.

column4: #### *He will come again to judge the living and the dead.*
column5: #### *He will come again to judge the living and the dead.*

column4: This points to the future return of Christ when He will bring final justice and restoration. Jesus will judge all people, rewarding the faithful and bringing justice to the unrepentant (2 Timothy 4:1). His return will fulfill God’s ultimate plan for creation, ushering in His eternal Kingdom of righteousness and peace. This hope encourages believers to live faithfully and expectantly, knowing their labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).

column4: #### *I believe in the Holy Spirit.*
column5: #### *I believe in the Holy Spirit.*

column4: The Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity, is God’s presence and power active in the world today. He convicts of sin, regenerates hearts, and empowers believers to live holy lives (John 16:8-13). The Spirit unites Christians as one body, the Church, and equips them with spiritual gifts for service (1 Corinthians 12:4-11). He is the Comforter, Advocate, and Guide, dwelling within believers as a seal of their eternal inheritance (Ephesians 1:13-14).

He is the Comforter, Advocate, and Guide, who dwells in believers and remains as the seal of their eternal inheritance (Ephesians 1:13-14).

column4: #### *The holy catholic Church, the communion of saints.*
column5: #### *The holy catholic Church, the communion of saints.*

column4: The "holy catholic Church" refers to the universal body of Christ, comprising all believers across time and space. The Church is set apart for God’s purposes, called to reflect His holiness and share the gospel. The "communion of saints" emphasizes the unity of all Christians, living and dead, as members of Christ’s body (Ephesians 4:4-6). This fellowship transcends earthly divisions, demonstrating the shared hope and mission of believers.

column4: #### *The forgiveness of sins.*
column5: #### *The forgiveness of sins.*

column4: This highlights the heart of the gospel: through Jesus’ sacrificial death, God offers complete forgiveness for sins to all who repent and believe (Ephesians 1:7). This forgiveness restores the broken relationship between humanity and God, removing guilt and shame. It also calls believers to extend forgiveness to others, reflecting the grace they have received (Matthew 6:14-15).

column4: #### *The resurrection of the body.*
column5: #### *The resurrection of the body.*

column4: Like Jesus, we will experience a bodily resurrection at the end of time. This resurrection will transform mortal, perishable bodies into glorified, imperishable ones fit for eternal life (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). It underscores the Christian hope of restoration, not just for individuals, but for all creation, as God makes all things new (Revelation 21:4-5).

column4: #### *And the life everlasting. Amen.*
column5: #### *And the life everlasting. Amen.*

column4: Eternal life with God is the ultimate promise of the Christian faith. This life begins now through a relationship with Christ and will be fully realized in the new heavens and new earth, where believers will dwell with God forever (John 3:16; Revelation 22:1-5). This closing affirmation reflects the joy and confidence of salvation, echoing the trust and hope expressed throughout the Creed.

column4: ## Conclusion
column5: ## Conclusion

column4: In the foundational truths expressed in the Apostles Creed, we see Jesus’ life and work as central to God’s plan for humanity. Each statement in the Creed captures key aspects of our belief in God, and who Jesus is-His divinity, humanity, mission, and ultimate triumph. These truths point to His unique role as the Mediator of the New Covenant. As Mediator He invites us to approach God with confidence, trusting in His perfect sacrifice and ongoing intercession. It calls us to worship Him as the rightful King and to follow His teachings as the ultimate Prophet. Ultimately, the study of Jesus leads to a deeper relationship with Him, transforming us into people who live in the light of His grace and truth.
column5: Among the basic truths expressed in the Apostles’ Creed, we find the life and work of Jesus at the center of God’s plan for humanity। In each statement of the creed are captured the key aspects of our belief about God, and who Jesus is-his divinity, humanity, mission, and final victory-are captured। These truths point to his unique role as the mediator of the new covenant। As mediator he invites us to come to God with confidence, trusting in his perfect sacrifice and ongoing intercession। This calls us to worship him as the rightful king and to follow his teachings as the supreme prophet। Ultimately, studying Jesus deepens our relationship with him, and transforms us into people who live in the light of his grace and truth।
